# Monitoring models in production {#sec-ch-ops-monitor}

> *"Your monitoring system should address two questions: what's broken, and
> why?"* — Rob Ewaschuk, in *Site Reliability Engineering*, 2016
> [@beyer2016, ch. 6]



::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- decide **what to monitor** in an ML service — golden signals, inputs,
  outputs, quality — and express objectives as **SLOs** with error budgets
  and burn rates;
- instrument a FastAPI service with **Prometheus** metrics (counters,
  gauges, histograms), query them with PromQL, and bound the error of
  **quantiles estimated from histogram buckets**;
- define **covariate, label and concept shift**, detect drift with the
  **population stability index** (proved to be a symmetric Kullback–Leibler
  divergence that can only shrink when bins are merged), the
  **Kolmogorov–Smirnov** test with a sample size from the **DKW** inequality,
  and the **χ²** test on predicted classes — controlling false alarms across
  windows;
- estimate how the class mix changes **without labels**, with black-box shift
  estimation and the EM adjustment of priors, and know their assumptions;
- detect changes as they happen with **CUSUM**, trading false alarms against
  detection delay;
- run a monitoring stack with **Docker Compose** — the service, Prometheus,
  Alertmanager — write **alert rules** with motivated thresholds, test them
  with `promtool`, and describe a **Grafana** dashboard and alert.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Topics covered
What to monitor in production; data drift and concept drift; Docker Compose;
Grafana dashboards; alerts and notifications.
:::

## What to monitor {#sec-ops-what-monitor}

### Four layers of signals

A model service can fail in ways an ordinary service cannot, so its
monitoring has more layers:

| Layer | Signals | Needs labels? | Reacts in |
|---|---|---|---|
| **service** | the four golden signals: **latency**, **traffic**, **errors**, **saturation** [@beyer2016, ch. 6] | no | seconds |
| **inputs** | text length, rate of unknown words, language, share of empty or truncated texts | no | minutes |
| **outputs** | distribution of predicted classes, mean confidence, share of low-confidence answers | no | minutes to hours |
| **quality** | accuracy, calibration, per-slice metrics on labelled samples | yes — often delayed | days |

The first layer says the service is up; only the others say it is *right*.
Labels arrive late, if ever (someone must annotate a sample of posts), so
the label-free signals of inputs and outputs are the early warnings, and
@sec-ops-drift, @sec-ops-label-shift and @sec-ops-cusum turn them into tests.

### Objectives: SLOs and error budgets

A **service level indicator** (SLI) is a measured quantity — the fraction of
requests answered successfully within 300 ms, say. A **service level
objective** (SLO) is a target for it over a window — 99.5 % over 30 days. The
complement is the **error budget**: $1 - 0.995 = 0.5\,\%$ of the requests may
fail without breaking the objective [@beyer2016, ch. 4]. The **burn rate** is
the observed bad fraction divided by the budget fraction: at burn rate 1 the
budget lasts exactly the window; at burn rate $r$ it lasts $1/r$ of it.

::: {#prp-ops-burn}
## Time to exhaust an error budget
With an SLO $s$ over a window of length $W$ and a constant bad-request
fraction $e > 0$, the budget is exhausted after
$$
T = W\,\frac{1 - s}{e} = \frac{W}{r}, \qquad r = \frac{e}{1 - s} .
$$
An alert on "burn rate above $r^\star$ measured over a window $\tau$" fires
only for incidents that would consume, if they lasted the whole SLO window, at
least $r^\star$ times the budget.
:::

*In one line:* the budget is a quantity of failures; dividing it by the rate
of failures gives the time left.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ops-burn
With traffic $\lambda$ the budget is $(1 - s)\lambda W$ bad requests;
failures accumulate at rate $e\lambda$, so the budget is gone after $(1 -
s)\lambda W/(e\lambda) = W(1 - s)/e$. The second sentence restates $r =
e/(1 - s)$. $\blacksquare$
:::

Google's SRE workbook recommends alerting on burn rates over two windows at
once — e.g. 14.4 over both the last hour and the last 5 minutes, which
pages when 2 % of a 30-day budget burns in an hour — so that alerts are both
significant and quick to reset [@beyer2018, ch. 5].

### Metrics with Prometheus

**Prometheus** stores **time series** — a metric name with labels, sampled
over time — that it collects by **scraping**: every few seconds it requests
`GET /metrics` from each target, which answers with the current values in a
simple text format [@prometheus2026]. Four metric types cover most needs:

- a **counter** only increases (requests served, predictions per label);
  queries look at its rate, `rate(x[5m])`, which also handles restarts;
- a **gauge** goes up and down (requests in flight, model load time);
- a **histogram** counts observations into cumulative buckets
  (`le` = "less than or equal") plus their sum and count — latencies, text
  lengths, confidences — and is aggregated across replicas;
- a **summary** computes quantiles in the client; they cannot be aggregated.

The service of @sec-ch-ops-serving has a hook (`OBSERVERS`) called with the
texts and probabilities of every prediction. An instrumented version adds a
middleware for request metrics, an observer for model metrics, and the
`/metrics` endpoint:


**`monitored.py`**

``` {.python}
"""The sentiment service with Prometheus metrics."""
import time

from prometheus_client import Counter, Gauge, Histogram, make_asgi_app

from app import LABELS, OBSERVERS, STATE, app

REQUESTS = Counter("sentiment_http_requests_total", "HTTP requests", ["path", "status"])
LATENCY = Histogram("sentiment_http_request_seconds", "Request latency", ["path"],
                    buckets=(0.002, 0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0))
PREDICTIONS = Counter("sentiment_predictions_total", "Predicted labels", ["label"])
CONFIDENCE = Histogram("sentiment_confidence", "Largest class probability",
                       buckets=(0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99))
LENGTH = Histogram("sentiment_text_length_chars", "Characters per text",
                   buckets=(10, 20, 30, 40, 60, 80, 120, 200, 280))
MODEL_INFO = Gauge("sentiment_model_info", "Served model version", ["version"])


def observe(texts, proba):
    for text, p in zip(texts, proba, strict=True):
        PREDICTIONS.labels(LABELS[int(p.argmax())]).inc()
        CONFIDENCE.observe(float(p.max()))
        LENGTH.observe(len(text))
    MODEL_INFO.labels(STATE["version"]).set(1)


OBSERVERS.append(observe)


@app.middleware("http")
async def record(request, call_next):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    response = await call_next(request)
    path = request.url.path
    if path != "/metrics":
        LATENCY.labels(path).observe(time.perf_counter() - start)
        REQUESTS.labels(path, str(response.status_code)).inc()
    return response


app.mount("/metrics", make_asgi_app())
```

Every histogram bucket is **cumulative**: `le="0.9"` counts the observations
$\le 0.9$, and the `+Inf` bucket equals the count. Prometheus estimates a
quantile from the buckets with `histogram_quantile`, by linear interpolation
inside the bucket that contains it.

::: {#prp-ops-hist-quantile}
## Quantiles from buckets
Let the buckets have upper bounds $b_0 < b_1 < \dots < b_K$ and cumulative
counts $N_0 \le \dots \le N_K = N$, and let the $\phi$-quantile's rank $r =
\phi N$ fall in bucket $j$ ($N_{j-1} < r \le N_j$). Prometheus returns
$$
\hat q_\phi = b_{j-1} + (b_j - b_{j-1})\,\frac{r - N_{j-1}}{N_j - N_{j-1}} ,
$$ {#eq-ops-hist-quantile}
and the empirical $\phi$-quantile $q_\phi$ of the observations lies in the
same bucket, so $|\hat q_\phi - q_\phi| \le b_j - b_{j-1}$.
:::

*In one line:* the bucket that contains the rank is known exactly; inside it,
the position is a guess — so the error is at most the bucket's width.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ops-hist-quantile
The empirical quantile is the $\lceil r\rceil$-th smallest observation; since
$N_{j-1} < r \le N_j$, exactly $N_{j-1}$ observations are $\le b_{j-1}$ and
$N_j$ are $\le b_j$, so it lies in $(b_{j-1}, b_j]$. The formula interpolates
linearly between the bucket's bounds, so $\hat q_\phi \in [b_{j-1}, b_j]$ too.
Two points of an interval of length $b_j - b_{j-1}$ are at most that far
apart. $\blacksquare$
:::

The practical consequence: put bucket boundaries densely **around the
values you alert on** — a latency SLO of 250 ms needs boundaries near 250 ms,
not only at 100 ms and 1 s.

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ops7-what-easy}
## Easy — buckets and budgets by hand
(a) A latency histogram has cumulative counts 500 at `le=0.05`, 900 at
`le=0.1`, 980 at `le=0.25`, 1 000 at `le=0.5`. Estimate the 95th percentile
with @eq-ops-hist-quantile and bound its error. (b) An SLO of 99.5 % over 30
days: how long does the budget last if 2 % of requests fail? What burn rate
is that?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
(a) The rank is $0.95 \times 1000 = 950$: which bucket contains it?
(b) $r = e/(1 - s)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#eb8a8423 .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
b = [0.0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5]; N = [0, 500, 900, 980, 1000]
r = 0.95 * N[-1]
j = next(i for i in range(1, len(N)) if N[i - 1] < r <= N[i])
q = b[j - 1] + (b[j] - b[j - 1]) * (r - N[j - 1]) / (N[j] - N[j - 1])
print(f"(a) p95 ≈ {q:.4f} s, error at most {b[j] - b[j - 1]:.2f} s")
e, s, W = 0.02, 0.995, 30
print(f"(b) burn rate {e / (1 - s):.1f}: budget gone after {W * (1 - s) / e:.1f} days")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
(a) p95 ≈ 0.1938 s, error at most 0.15 s
(b) burn rate 4.0: budget gone after 7.5 days
```
:::
:::


(a) Rank 950 falls in the bucket $(0.1, 0.25]$: the estimate is 0.194 s, but
the true value could be anywhere in that bucket — an error up to 150 ms. (b)
A burn rate of 4: the month's budget is gone in a week. A burn-rate alert at
14.4 would not fire for this slow leak; a second, lower threshold over a
longer window (e.g. 1 over 3 days) catches it.
:::

::: {#exr-ops7-what-medium}
## Medium — Prometheus for real
Start the instrumented service and a Prometheus server (the binary, on the
loopback interface) that scrapes it every second. Send traffic for 20
seconds, then query, through Prometheus's HTTP API: the request rate, the
share of each predicted label, and the 95th-percentile latency. Compare the
percentile with the one computed from the client-side measurements.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
`GET /api/v1/query?query=<PromQL>` returns JSON. Useful expressions:
`sum(rate(sentiment_http_requests_total[15s]))`,
`sum by (label) (rate(sentiment_predictions_total[15s]))`,
`histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(sentiment_http_request_seconds_bucket[15s])))`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#794b8e87 .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def start_prometheus(directory: Path, config: str, port: int):
    (directory / "prometheus.yml").write_text(textwrap.dedent(config))
    proc = subprocess.Popen([ob.tool("prometheus"), f"--config.file={directory / 'prometheus.yml'}",
                             f"--storage.tsdb.path={directory / 'data'}", f"--web.listen-address=127.0.0.1:{port}"],
                            stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL)
    ob.wait_port(port)
    return proc

def promql(port, expr):
    r = httpx.get(f"http://127.0.0.1:{port}/api/v1/query", params={"query": expr}).json()
    return {tuple(sorted(x["metric"].items())): float(x["value"][1]) for x in r["data"]["result"]}

prom_dir = ob.project("prometheus")
traffic = list(ob.make_posts(4000, seed=70).text)
client_lat = []
with ob.server("monitored:app", cwd=mon, env={"MODEL_VERSION": "v1"}) as (base, _):
    svc_port = int(base.rsplit(":", 1)[1])
    prom_port = ob.free_port()
    prom = start_prometheus(prom_dir, f"""
        global:
          scrape_interval: 1s
        scrape_configs:
          - job_name: sentiment
            static_configs:
              - targets: ["127.0.0.1:{svc_port}"]
    """, prom_port)
    with httpx.Client(base_url=base, timeout=5) as client:
        t_end = time.time() + 20
        i = 0
        while time.time() < t_end:
            t0 = time.perf_counter()
            client.post("/v1/predict", json={"texts": traffic[i % 4000: i % 4000 + 4]})
            client_lat.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
            i += 4
            time.sleep(0.01)
    time.sleep(2)
    rate = promql(prom_port, "sum(rate(sentiment_http_requests_total[15s]))")
    labels = promql(prom_port, "sum by (label) (rate(sentiment_predictions_total[15s]))")
    p95 = promql(prom_port, "histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(sentiment_http_request_seconds_bucket[15s])))")
    prom.terminate()
total = sum(labels.values())
print(f"request rate {list(rate.values())[0]:.1f}/s")
print("label shares:", {dict(k)["label"]: round(v / total, 3) for k, v in labels.items()})
print(f"p95 latency: Prometheus {1e3 * list(p95.values())[0]:.1f} ms, client side {1e3 * np.quantile(client_lat, 0.95):.1f} ms")
```

```
label shares: {'neutral': 0.403, 'positive': 0.294, 'negative': 0.303}
p95 latency: Prometheus 4.9 ms, client side 7.2 ms
```

Prometheus reports the request rate, the label mix (close to the generator's
30/40/30 priors) and a 95th percentile that differs from the client-side one:
the server measures less (no network, no client), and the estimate is
interpolated inside a bucket whose width bounds its error
(@prp-ops-hist-quantile). The rate window must contain several scrapes —
`rate()` over a window shorter than two scrape intervals returns nothing.
:::

::: {#exr-ops7-what-hard}
## Hard — buckets for an SLO
The SLO says: 95 % of prediction requests within 6 ms on the build machine.
Choose histogram buckets so that `histogram_quantile(0.95, …)` decides
reliably whether the SLO is met — i.e. the estimate's error is at most
0.5 ms near 6 ms — with no more than ten buckets. Check your choice by replaying the
client-side latencies of the previous exercise through two histograms (the
service's default buckets and yours) and computing @eq-ops-hist-quantile for
both.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Only the bucket that contains the 95th percentile matters for its error;
boundaries far from 6 ms can be coarse. Simulate the histogram with
`np.searchsorted` on the sorted latencies.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#482383b5 .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def hist_quantile(values, bounds, phi):
    bounds = np.asarray(bounds, float)
    cum = np.array([np.sum(np.asarray(values) <= u) for u in bounds])
    r = phi * len(values)
    j = int(np.searchsorted(cum, r))          # first bucket with cumulative count >= r
    lo = bounds[j - 1] if j > 0 else 0.0
    prev = cum[j - 1] if j > 0 else 0
    return lo + (bounds[j] - lo) * (r - prev) / (cum[j] - prev), bounds[j] - lo

lat = np.array(client_lat)
default = [0.002, 0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, np.inf]
mine = [0.002, 0.004, 0.005, 0.0055, 0.006, 0.0065, 0.007, 0.01, 0.025, np.inf]
print(f"true p95 {1e3 * np.quantile(lat, 0.95):.2f} ms; SLO 6 ms")
widths = {}
for name, bounds in (("default", default), ("dense near 6 ms", mine)):
    q, width = hist_quantile(lat, bounds, 0.95)
    widths[name] = width
    print(f"{name:16s} estimate {1e3 * q:.2f} ms, bucket width {1e3 * width:.1f} ms")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
true p95 7.19 ms; SLO 6 ms
default          estimate 9.64 ms, bucket width 5.0 ms
dense near 6 ms  estimate 7.61 ms, bucket width 3.0 ms
```
:::
:::


With the default buckets the 95th percentile falls in a bucket
5 ms wide, so an estimate near 6 ms
could be off by more than the margin that decides whether the SLO holds; with
boundaries every half millisecond around 6 ms the error is bounded by
3\.0 ms (if the percentile
falls there), using the same number of buckets. (On a slower or faster
machine the percentile moves; the bucket design should follow the SLO, not
the current measurement.) Each bucket is a separate time series for
Prometheus, so adding many is not free; placing them where the decisions are
made is.
:::

## Data drift and concept drift {#sec-ops-drift}

### Three kinds of shift

Write the joint distribution of an input $X$ and its label $Y$ in two ways,
$P(X, Y) = P(X)\,P(Y \mid X) = P(Y)\,P(X \mid Y)$. When production data come
from $P_t$ instead of the training distribution $P_s$, three cases are
distinguished [@morenotorres2012; @quinonero2009]:

- **covariate shift**: $P_t(X) \ne P_s(X)$, but $P_t(Y \mid X) = P_s(Y \mid
  X)$ — new topics, longer posts, slang the model never saw; the right answer
  for each post is unchanged;
- **label (prior) shift**: $P_t(Y) \ne P_s(Y)$, but $P_t(X \mid Y) =
  P_s(X \mid Y)$ — the public mood turns negative after an outage; negative
  posts look as before, there are just more of them;
- **concept shift**: $P_t(Y \mid X) \ne P_s(Y \mid X)$ — the same words now
  mean something else ("sick" as praise, a product name that becomes a
  joke, irony spreading). This is the dangerous one: inputs may look
  unchanged, and only labels reveal it.

"Data drift" usually refers to the first two, observable without labels;
"concept drift" to the third. The synthetic posts make each kind a switch:

::: {#0a1b8a04 .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
shifts = {
    "none": {},
    "covariate: unseen slang": {"slang_rate": 0.8},
    "covariate: new topics": {"topics": ob.NEW_TOPICS},
    "label: 60 % negative": {"prior": (0.6, 0.2, 0.2)},
    "concept: 5 words flip": {"swap": {w: 0 for w in ("cheap", "fast", "smooth", "perfect", "awesome")}},
}
rows = []
for name, kw in shifts.items():
    d = ob.make_posts(4000, seed=500, **kw)
    proba = model.predict_proba(d.text)
    rows.append({"shift": name, "accuracy": accuracy_score(d.label, proba.argmax(1)),
                 "mean length": d.text.str.len().mean(), "mean confidence": proba.max(1).mean(),
                 "share predicted negative": np.mean(proba.argmax(1) == 0)})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3).to_string(index=False))
```

```
                  shift  accuracy  mean length  mean confidence  share predicted negative
                   none     0.928       36.396            0.861                     0.299
covariate: unseen slang     0.915       41.148            0.844                     0.298
  covariate: new topics     0.931       36.816            0.897                     0.296
   label: 60 % negative     0.925       36.737            0.852                     0.587
  concept: 5 words flip     0.864       36.530            0.854                     0.243
```
:::
:::


Each shift leaves a different footprint. Slang makes the posts longer (the
inserted word) and costs a little accuracy; new topics leave the length and the
accuracy unchanged — the model never relied on topics — but make it *more*
confident (the new topic words are unknown, so the polar words weigh more);
label shift doubles the share of predicted negatives while accuracy stays;
the concept shift costs six points of accuracy, with inputs and confidence
unchanged and, here, a visible drop of predicted negatives (posts that became
negative are still predicted positive). No single monitor sees everything.

### The population stability index

A popular drift score compares the distribution of a quantity — a feature,
the model's confidence — in a **reference** sample and a **current** sample,
both binned into $B$ bins with proportions $q_i$ (reference) and $p_i$
(current):
$$
\mathrm{PSI} = \sum_{i=1}^{B} (p_i - q_i)\ln\frac{p_i}{q_i} .
$$ {#eq-ops-psi}

::: {#prp-ops-psi}
## PSI is Jeffreys' divergence, and binning can only hide drift
(i) $\mathrm{PSI} = \mathrm{KL}(p\,\|\,q) + \mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p)$, the
symmetrised Kullback–Leibler divergence introduced by Jeffreys
[@jeffreys1946; @kullback1951]; hence $\mathrm{PSI} \ge 0$, with equality iff
$p = q$. (ii) Merging bins never increases the PSI: if $p', q'$ are obtained
by summing groups of bins of $p, q$, then $\mathrm{PSI}(p', q') \le
\mathrm{PSI}(p, q)$.
:::

*In one line:* PSI measures how surprised each distribution is by the other;
coarse bins blur differences, never invent them.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ops-psi
(i) $\mathrm{KL}(p\|q) + \mathrm{KL}(q\|p) = \sum_i p_i \ln(p_i/q_i) + \sum_i
q_i\ln(q_i/p_i) = \sum_i (p_i - q_i)\ln(p_i/q_i)$. Each KL is $\ge 0$ by
Gibbs' inequality ($\ln x \le x - 1$ gives $-\mathrm{KL}(p\|q) = \sum p_i
\ln(q_i/p_i) \le \sum (q_i - p_i) = 0$), with equality iff $p = q$; so is the
sum — indeed every term $(p_i - q_i)\ln(p_i/q_i)$ is $\ge 0$ because both
factors have the same sign. (ii) It suffices to merge two bins. By the
**log-sum inequality**, $a_1\ln\frac{a_1}{b_1} + a_2\ln\frac{a_2}{b_2} \ge
(a_1 + a_2)\ln\frac{a_1 + a_2}{b_1 + b_2}$ for positive $a, b$ (a consequence
of the convexity of $t \mapsto t\ln t$). Applied with $(a, b) = (p, q)$ it
shows that $\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)$ does not increase when the two bins are
merged; applied with $(a, b) = (q, p)$, neither does $\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)$; so
neither does their sum. $\blacksquare$
:::

Two consequences matter in practice. The value of the PSI **depends on the
binning** — ten quantile bins of the reference are customary, but any change
of bins changes the number — so a PSI threshold is meaningful only with its
binning. And the widely quoted thresholds — below 0.1 "stable", 0.1–0.25
"some change", above 0.25 "significant shift" — are **industry folklore**,
from credit scoring practice [@siddiqi2006], not results of a theory: they
ignore the sample size (a PSI of 0.05 is noise with 200 posts and a real
change with 200 000) and the binning. A PSI is a measure of *size*; whether a
change is *real* is what the tests below answer.

The widget computes the PSI of the model's confidence between a reference
sample and samples with an increasing amount of unseen slang, for two
binnings.

::: {#117e6e59 .cell execution_count=8}

### Tests: Kolmogorov–Smirnov and χ²

For a continuous quantity, the **two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic**
is the largest vertical distance between the two empirical CDFs, $D =
\sup_x |\hat F_n(x) - \hat G_m(x)|$; under "same distribution" its law does
not depend on the distribution, which gives exact p-values
(`scipy.stats.ks_2samp`). How many observations does a window need to see a
shift of a given size? The **Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz** inequality, with
the optimal constant found by Massart, answers with a bound that holds for
every $n$ [@dvoretzky1956; @massart1990]:
$$
P\Bigl(\sup_x |\hat F_n(x) - F(x)| > \varepsilon\Bigr) \le 2e^{-2n\varepsilon^2}.
$$ {#eq-ops-dkw}

::: {#prp-ops-ks-size}
## A sample size for detecting a shift
Let both samples have size $n$, and set $\varepsilon = \sqrt{\ln(4/\alpha)/(2n)}$.
The test that signals drift when $D > 2\varepsilon$ has false-alarm
probability at most $\alpha$; if the true distributions satisfy $\sup_x|F(x)
- G(x)| \ge \delta$ with $\delta > 4\varepsilon$ — that is, $n > 8\ln(4/\alpha)/\delta^2$
— it detects the shift with probability at least $1 - \alpha$.
:::

*In one line:* each empirical CDF is within $\varepsilon$ of its truth with
high probability, so two equal distributions look at most $2\varepsilon$
apart and two distributions $\delta$ apart look at least $\delta -
2\varepsilon$ apart.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ops-ks-size
By @eq-ops-dkw and the union bound, with probability at least $1 - 4e^{-2n
\varepsilon^2} = 1 - \alpha$ both $\sup|\hat F_n - F| \le \varepsilon$ and
$\sup|\hat G_n - G| \le \varepsilon$. On that event, by the triangle
inequality, $|D - \sup_x|F - G|| \le 2\varepsilon$. If $F = G$, then $D \le
2\varepsilon$: a false alarm has probability at most $\alpha$. If $\sup|F -
G| \ge \delta > 4\varepsilon$, then $D \ge \delta - 2\varepsilon > 2\varepsilon$:
the shift is detected with probability at least $1 - \alpha$. $\blacksquare$
:::

The bound is conservative — the exact KS test is more powerful — but it is
valid for any distribution and any $n$, and it shows the scaling: halving the
detectable shift quadruples the window.

For the **predicted classes**, a categorical quantity, the natural test
compares observed counts $O_k$ in a window of $n$ predictions with the counts
$E_k = n\pi_k$ expected from the reference shares $\pi_k$ with **Pearson's
statistic** $X^2 = \sum_k (O_k - E_k)^2/E_k$, approximately $\chi^2_{K-1}$
under "no change" [@pearson1900].

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Why $X^2$ is approximately $\chi^2_{K-1}$
Let $Z_k = (O_k - n\pi_k)/\sqrt{n\pi_k}$, so $X^2 = \|Z\|^2$. The counts are
multinomial, so by the multivariate central limit theorem $Z$ is approximately
normal with mean 0 and covariance $I - \sqrt\pi\sqrt\pi^{\top}$ (from
$\mathrm{Var}(O_k) = n\pi_k(1 - \pi_k)$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(O_j, O_k) =
-n\pi_j\pi_k$). That matrix is the orthogonal projection onto the hyperplane
orthogonal to the unit vector $\sqrt\pi$, of rank $K - 1$; a standard normal
vector projected onto a $(K-1)$-dimensional subspace has squared norm
$\chi^2_{K-1}$. $\blacksquare$
:::

### Many windows, many false alarms

A monitor runs a test on every window — every hour, say. With level $\alpha$
per window and no drift at all, the expected number of false alarms per day is
$24\alpha$, and the probability of at least one is $1 - (1 - \alpha)^{24}$:
at $\alpha = 0.05$, about 70 %. Two remedies: a smaller per-window level
(Bonferroni, $\alpha/m$ for $m$ tests per period, @exr-ops4-flaky; or the less
conservative Benjamini–Hochberg procedure when many features are tested at
once, which controls the expected share of false alarms among all alarms
[@benjamini1995]), or a sequential method that accumulates evidence over
windows (@sec-ops-cusum).

::: {#16c8599a .cell execution_count=9}
``` {.python .cell-code}
reference = ob.make_posts(5000, seed=700)
ref_len = reference.text.str.len().to_numpy()
ref_pred = model.predict(reference.text)
ref_share = np.bincount(ref_pred, minlength=3) / len(ref_pred)

def window_tests(posts):
    pred = model.predict(posts.text)
    counts = np.bincount(pred, minlength=3)
    return {"KS length p": ks_2samp(ref_len, posts.text.str.len()).pvalue,
            "chi2 classes p": chisquare(counts, ref_share * counts.sum()).pvalue}

for name, kw in shifts.items():
    res = window_tests(ob.make_posts(500, seed=800, **kw))
    print(f"{name:26s} " + "  ".join(f"{k} = {v:.2g}" for k, v in res.items()))
```

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ops7-drift-easy}
## Easy — PSI and KS by hand
Reference shares of predicted classes (negative, neutral, positive):
$(0.30, 0.40, 0.30)$; current window: $(0.45, 0.30, 0.25)$. Compute the PSI
and check it equals $\mathrm{KL}(p\|q) + \mathrm{KL}(q\|p)$. Then, for two
samples of text lengths `[12, 15, 20, 22, 30]` and `[18, 25, 27, 33, 41]`,
compute the KS statistic $D$ by hand (the largest gap between the two step
functions).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
For KS, evaluate both empirical CDFs at every observed value; the supremum is
attained at one of them.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#4edb6b1b .cell execution_count=10}
``` {.python .cell-code}
q_ = np.array([0.30, 0.40, 0.30]); p_ = np.array([0.45, 0.30, 0.25])
psi = np.sum((p_ - q_) * np.log(p_ / q_))
kl = lambda a, b: np.sum(a * np.log(a / b))
print(f"PSI = {psi:.4f}, KL(p||q) + KL(q||p) = {kl(p_, q_) + kl(q_, p_):.4f}")
a, b = np.array([12, 15, 20, 22, 30]), np.array([18, 25, 27, 33, 41])
grid = np.sort(np.r_[a, b])
gaps = [abs(np.mean(a <= x) - np.mean(b <= x)) for x in grid]
print(f"D = {max(gaps):.1f} at x = {grid[int(np.argmax(gaps))]}; scipy: {ks_2samp(a, b).statistic:.1f}, p = {ks_2samp(a, b).pvalue:.3f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
PSI = 0.0987, KL(p||q) + KL(q||p) = 0.0987
D = 0.6 at x = 22; scipy: 0.6, p = 0.357
```
:::
:::


PSI ≈ 0.099 — just "stable" by the folklore thresholds, although the
negative share rose by half; whether that is significant depends on the window size

::: {#exr-ops7-drift-medium}
## Medium — false alarms over a day
Simulate 24 hourly windows of 300 posts **without** any drift and run the
χ² test on the predicted classes in each, at $\alpha = 0.05$. Repeat the day
500 times and estimate the probability of at least one false alarm per day,
with and without the Bonferroni correction. Then insert label shift (60 %
negative) from hour 12 and estimate how often each version detects it within
three hours.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
To save time, simulate the predicted counts directly: under no drift they are
multinomial with the reference shares; under label shift, with the shares the
model predicts on shifted data (measure them once).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#a420cac7 .cell execution_count=11}
``` {.python .cell-code}
rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
shifted_share = np.bincount(model.predict(ob.make_posts(5000, seed=801, prior=(0.6, 0.2, 0.2)).text), minlength=3) / 5000

def day(alpha, shift_from=None, n=300):
    alarms = []
    for h in range(24):
        share = shifted_share if shift_from is not None and h >= shift_from else ref_share
        counts = rng.multinomial(n, share)
        alarms.append(chisquare(counts, ref_share * n).pvalue < alpha)
    return np.array(alarms)

for name, a in (("alpha = 0.05", 0.05), ("Bonferroni 0.05/24", 0.05 / 24)):
    false_day = np.mean([day(a).any() for _ in range(500)])
    detect = np.mean([day(a, shift_from=12)[12:15].any() for _ in range(500)])
    print(f"{name:20s} P(false alarm in a quiet day) {false_day:.2f}; P(detect the shift within 3 h) {detect:.2f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
alpha = 0.05         P(false alarm in a quiet day) 0.70; P(detect the shift within 3 h) 1.00
Bonferroni 0.05/24   P(false alarm in a quiet day) 0.05; P(detect the shift within 3 h) 1.00
```
:::
:::


At 5 % per window, a quiet day raises at least one alarm most of the time —
people learn to ignore such a monitor. With Bonferroni the daily false-alarm
probability falls below 5 %, and this large label shift is still caught
within three hours. Smaller shifts would need larger windows or the
cumulative evidence of @sec-ops-cusum.
:::

::: {#exr-ops7-drift-hard}
## Hard — which monitor sees which shift?
For each of the four shifts of this section (slang, new topics, label, concept)
and for "none", run on 50 windows of 500 posts: the KS test on text length,
the KS test on confidence, the χ² test on predicted classes, the PSI of the
confidence (10 quantile bins), and — assuming 50 labelled posts per window —
a test that accuracy has dropped below the reference (one-sided, exact
binomial). Report the detection rate of each monitor for each shift at a
per-window level of 1 %, and propose a minimal set of monitors that covers all
four shifts.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Compute the reference quantities (lengths, confidences, class shares,
accuracy) once on a large reference sample. For the accuracy test, the number
of correct answers among 50 is binomial with the reference accuracy under "no
change". The PSI has no p-value: decide a threshold by looking at its values
under "none".
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#1cab40f5 .cell execution_count=12}
``` {.python .cell-code}

ref_conf_all, ref_acc = ref_proba.max(1), accuracy_score(reference.label, ref_proba.argmax(1))
edges = np.quantile(ref_conf_all, np.linspace(0, 1, 11)[1:-1])
q_bins = np.bincount(np.searchsorted(edges, ref_conf_all), minlength=10) / len(ref_conf_all)

def monitors(posts, rng):
    proba = model.predict_proba(posts.text)
    conf, pred = proba.max(1), proba.argmax(1)
    p_bins = np.maximum(np.bincount(np.searchsorted(edges, conf), minlength=10) / len(conf), 1e-6)
    lab = rng.choice(len(posts), 50, replace=False)
    correct = int(np.sum(pred[lab] == posts.label.to_numpy()[lab]))
    return {"KS length": ks_2samp(ref_len, posts.text.str.len()).pvalue < 0.01,
            "KS confidence": ks_2samp(ref_conf_all, conf).pvalue < 0.01,
            "chi2 classes": chisquare(np.bincount(pred, minlength=3), ref_share * len(pred)).pvalue < 0.01,
            "PSI conf > 0.1": float(np.sum((p_bins - q_bins) * np.log(p_bins / q_bins))) > 0.1,
            "accuracy (50 labels)": binom.cdf(correct, 50, ref_acc) < 0.01}
```

common mistake is to monitor only the inputs and conclude "no drift" while the
concept has moved.

## Estimating label shift without labels {#sec-ops-label-shift}

### The share of negative posts, corrected

The share of posts *predicted* negative is a biased estimate of the share
that *is* negative: errors move posts between classes, and the bias changes
with the class mix. Under **label shift** ($P_t(X \mid Y) = P_s(X \mid Y)$)
the bias can be removed.

::: {#thm-ops-bbse}
## Black-box shift estimation
Let $\hat y = f(x)$ be any fixed classifier, $C_{ij} = P_s(\hat y = i \mid
y = j)$ its confusion matrix normalised by true class on the source
distribution, $\mu_i = P_t(\hat y = i)$ the distribution of its predictions on
the target, and $q_j = P_t(y = j)$ the target priors. Under label shift,
$$
\mu = C q, \qquad\text{so, if } C \text{ is invertible,}\qquad q = C^{-1}\mu ,
$$ {#eq-ops-bbse}
and the importance weights are $w_j = q_j / p_j$ with $p_j = P_s(y = j)$
[@lipton2018].
:::

*In one line:* how the classifier errs given the true class is the same in
training and in production — only the class mix changed — so the observed
prediction mix is a known linear mixture of the unknown class mix.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-ops-bbse
By total probability, $\mu_i = \sum_j P_t(\hat y = i \mid y = j)P_t(y = j)$.
Since $\hat y$ is a function of $x$ and $P_t(x \mid y) = P_s(x \mid y)$, also
$P_t(\hat y = i \mid y = j) = P_s(\hat y = i \mid y = j) = C_{ij}$. Hence
$\mu = Cq$, and $q = C^{-1}\mu$ when $C$ is invertible. $\blacksquare$
:::

In practice $C$ is estimated on a labelled validation set from the source and
$\mu$ on unlabelled production data; the estimate inherits their noise, and
it is poor when $C$ is nearly singular (a classifier that confuses two classes
cannot separate their shares). It can also return small negative values,
which are clipped and renormalised.

A second method uses the model's **probabilities** instead of its decisions.

::: {#prp-ops-em-prior}
## EM adjustment of priors
If $p_s(y \mid x)$ is calibrated on the source and only the priors change,
then $p_t(y \mid x) \propto p_s(y \mid x)\,q_y/p_y$. The iteration
$$
q^{(k+1)}_y = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\frac{p_s(y \mid x_i)\,q^{(k)}_y/p_y}{\sum_{y'} p_s(y' \mid x_i)\,q^{(k)}_{y'}/p_{y'}}
$$ {#eq-ops-em}
never decreases the likelihood of the unlabelled target sample, and its
fixed points are the stationary points of that likelihood [@saerens2002].
:::

*In one line:* re-weight each post's probabilities by the ratio of new to old
priors, average them to get new priors, and repeat — expectation-maximisation
for the mixture weights.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ops-em-prior
By Bayes' rule $p_t(y \mid x) = p_t(x \mid y)q_y/p_t(x)$ and $p_t(x \mid y)
= p_s(x \mid y) = p_s(y \mid x)p_s(x)/p_y$, so $p_t(y \mid x) \propto
p_s(y \mid x)q_y/p_y$, normalised over $y$. The target density of $x$ is a
mixture $\sum_y q_y p_s(x \mid y)$ with known components and unknown weights
$q$; the E-step computes the responsibilities $p_t(y \mid x_i)$ under the
current $q^{(k)}$, and the M-step maximises the expected complete-data
log-likelihood $\sum_i\sum_y p_t(y \mid x_i)\log q_y$ over the simplex, whose
solution is the average responsibility — @eq-ops-em. EM never decreases the
observed-data likelihood [@dempster1977]; at a fixed point, the
Lagrangian stationarity conditions of the likelihood over the simplex hold,
since they reduce to the same averaging equation. $\blacksquare$
:::

EM needs calibrated probabilities (@sec-ops-calibration); BBSE needs only a
fixed classifier and an invertible confusion matrix. Both fail under concept
shift, where $P(x \mid y)$ changes. Let us compare them with the naive
"share of predictions". The local model is so accurate against the *true*
sentiment (its errors are mostly the annotators') that the naive share is
nearly right; to see the bias, take a quick classifier — unigrams, trained on
400 posts — and a carefully annotated validation set (`noise=0`: the true
sentiment), and measure the shares against the true sentiment:

::: {#960fc3ad .cell execution_count=13}

``` {.python .cell-code}
from scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar
small = ob.make_posts(400, seed=3)
quick = ob.train_model(small.text, small.label, ngram=(1, 1), C=1.0)

print(f"accuracy of the quick model against the true sentiment: {np.mean(quick.predict(valid.text) == y_val):.3f}")

z_val = quick.decision_function(valid.text)
T_cal = minimize_scalar(lambda T: -log_softmax(z_val / T, 1)[np.arange(len(y_val)), y_val].mean(),
                        bounds=(0.05, 20), method="bounded").x       # temperature scaling (@sec-ops-calibration)

def bbse(texts):
    mu = np.bincount(quick.predict(texts), minlength=3) / len(texts)
    q = np.clip(np.linalg.solve(C, mu), 0, None)
    return q / q.sum()

def em_priors(texts, iters=300):
    post = softmax(quick.decision_function(texts) / T_cal, axis=1)
    q = p_src.copy()
    for _ in range(iters):
        adj = post * q / p_src
        adj /= adj.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
        q = adj.mean(axis=0)
    return q

for truth in ((0.3, 0.4, 0.3), (0.6, 0.2, 0.2), (0.1, 0.3, 0.6)):
    d = ob.make_posts(3000, seed=720, prior=truth, noise=0)
    naive = np.bincount(quick.predict(d.text), minlength=3) / len(d)
    actual = np.bincount(d.label, minlength=3) / len(d)
    print(f"true {np.round(actual, 3)}  naive {np.round(naive, 3)}  BBSE {np.round(bbse(d.text), 3)}  EM {np.round(em_priors(d.text), 3)}")
```

## Easy — two classes by hand
A spam filter has, on validation data, $P(\hat y = \text{spam} \mid

spam? Why is the naive answer (23 %) wrong, and in which direction?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
$0.23 = 0.9\,q + 0.05\,(1 - q)$: solve for $q$.

``` {.python .cell-code}
C2 = np.array([[0.9, 0.05], [0.1, 0.95]])     # columns: true spam, true ham; rows: predicted spam, ham
print(np.linalg.solve(C2, [0.23, 0.77]))
```

```
[0.2118 0.7882]
```
:::
:::


$q = (0.23 - 0.05)/(0.9 - 0.05) \approx 0.212$: 21 % spam. The naive 23 %
counts the 5 % of ham wrongly flagged and misses the 10 % of spam let
through; with few spam messages the false positives dominate, so the naive
share is too high. The correction needs $C$ to be invertible: here the
classifier's two columns are clearly different ($0.9 \ne 0.05$).
:::

::: {#exr-ops7-ls-medium}
## Medium — BBSE with intervals
Estimate the share of negative posts with BBSE on windows of 300, 1 000 and
3 000 unlabelled posts whose true negative share is 0.5, and give a 90 %
interval by the bootstrap (resample the window and the validation set). How
does the width scale with the window size?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Both $\hat C$ and $\hat\mu$ are estimates: resample both in each bootstrap
replicate. The width should scale roughly like $1/\sqrt n$ once the window
dominates the error.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#dc81e858 .cell execution_count=16}
``` {.python .cell-code}
rng = np.random.default_rng(12)
val_pred, val_true = quick.predict(valid.text), y_val

def bbse_from(pred_window, vp, vt):
    Cb = np.zeros((3, 3))
    for j in range(3):
        Cb[:, j] = np.bincount(vp[vt == j], minlength=3) / max(np.sum(vt == j), 1)
    q = np.clip(np.linalg.solve(Cb, np.bincount(pred_window, minlength=3) / len(pred_window)), 0, None)
    return q / q.sum()

for n in (300, 1000, 3000):
    w = ob.make_posts(n, seed=740 + n, prior=(0.5, 0.25, 0.25), noise=0)
    wp = quick.predict(w.text)
    est = bbse_from(wp, val_pred, val_true)[0]
    boots = []
    for _ in range(300):
        i = rng.integers(0, n, n); k = rng.integers(0, len(val_pred), len(val_pred))
        boots.append(bbse_from(wp[i], val_pred[k], val_true[k])[0])
    lo, hi = np.quantile(boots, [0.05, 0.95])
    print(f"n = {n:4d}: estimate {est:.3f}, 90% interval [{lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f}], width {hi - lo:.3f}, true {np.mean(w.label == 0):.3f}")
```

## Detecting change as it happens: CUSUM {#sec-ops-cusum}

### Accumulating small evidence

Window tests look at each window separately; a small, persistent change
— two extra points of negative posts — is invisible in any single window. The
**cumulative sum** procedure of Page accumulates evidence across
observations [@page1954]. For observations $x_1, x_2, \dots$ (one per batch,
e.g. the share of negative predictions), a reference value $\mu_0$ and an
allowance $k \ge 0$:
$$
S_0 = 0, \qquad S_t = \max\bigl(0,\; S_{t-1} + x_t - \mu_0 - k\bigr), \qquad
\text{alarm when } S_t > h .
$$ {#eq-ops-cusum}
Each observation above $\mu_0 + k$ adds to $S$, each below subtracts, and
$S$ never goes below zero — it forgets good news.

::: {#prp-ops-cusum}
## What CUSUM computes, and how fast it reacts
(i) $S_t = \max_{0 \le s \le t}\sum_{i = s+1}^{t}(x_i - \mu_0 - k)$: the
largest excess accumulated over any recent stretch, maximised over the
unknown change point. (ii) If after a change the observations are
independent with mean $\mu_1 > \mu_0 + k$, then $E[S_{\tau + m}] \ge m(\mu_1 -
\mu_0 - k)$ for the change time $\tau$, so the expected detection delay is
about $h/(\mu_1 - \mu_0 - k)$ — linear in the threshold — whereas the mean
time between false alarms grows exponentially in $h$ [@siegmund1985, ch. 2].
:::

*In one line:* CUSUM keeps the best "a change started at $s$" score for all
$s$ at once; raising the threshold delays detection linearly but postpones
false alarms exponentially.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-ops-cusum
(i) By induction. For $t = 0$ both sides are 0 (empty sum). If $S_{t-1} =
\max_{s \le t-1}\sum_{s+1}^{t-1} z_i$ with $z_i = x_i - \mu_0 - k$, then
$\max_{s \le t}\sum_{s+1}^{t} z_i = \max\bigl(0, \max_{s \le t-1}\sum_{s+1}^{t-1}
z_i + z_t\bigr) = \max(0, S_{t-1} + z_t) = S_t$ (the $s = t$ term is the empty
sum). (ii) By (i) with $s = \tau$, $S_{\tau + m} \ge \sum_{i=\tau+1}^{\tau +
m} z_i$, whose expectation is $m(\mu_1 - \mu_0 - k)$; the statistic therefore
drifts upward at least at that rate and crosses $h$ after about $h/(\mu_1 -
\mu_0 - k)$ steps. The exponential growth of the in-control run length is a
classical result of random-walk theory (Wald's identity applied to the
excursions of $S$ above zero), which we use without proof, citing
@siegmund1985. $\blacksquare$
:::

The **Page–Hinkley** test is the same idea written with the running mean
instead of a fixed $\mu_0$ [@hinkley1971]. The choice of $k$ tunes CUSUM to a
target change: $k$ halfway between $\mu_0$ and the smallest $\mu_1$ worth
detecting is the classical choice for normal observations.

::: {#d3c9153b .cell execution_count=18}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def cusum(x, mu0, k, h):
    s, path, alarm = 0.0, [], None
    for t, v in enumerate(x):
        s = max(0.0, s + v - mu0 - k)
        path.append(s)
        if alarm is None and s > h:
            alarm = t
    return np.array(path), alarm

rng = np.random.default_rng(13)
batch = 200
p_neg_before = ref_share[0]
p_neg_after = np.bincount(model.predict(ob.make_posts(5000, seed=780, prior=(0.36, 0.36, 0.28)).text), minlength=3)[0] / 5000
x = np.r_[rng.binomial(batch, p_neg_before, 150), rng.binomial(batch, p_neg_after, 100)] / batch
path, alarm = cusum(x, mu0=p_neg_before, k=(p_neg_after - p_neg_before) / 2, h=0.15)
chi_alarm = next((t for t, v in enumerate(x) if chisquare([v * batch, (1 - v) * batch],
                  [p_neg_before * batch, (1 - p_neg_before) * batch]).pvalue < 0.05 / 250), None)
print(f"predicted-negative share: {p_neg_before:.3f} before, {p_neg_after:.3f} after the change at batch 150")
print(f"CUSUM alarm at batch {alarm}; per-batch chi-square test (Bonferroni) alarm at batch {chi_alarm}")
```

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ops7-cusum-easy}
## Easy — CUSUM by hand
Shares of negative predictions in ten batches: `0.30, 0.28, 0.33, 0.31, 0.36,
0.35, 0.37, 0.34, 0.38, 0.36`. With $\mu_0 = 0.30$, $k = 0.02$, $h = 0.1$,
compute $S_t$ step by step and the alarm time. Check (i) of
@prp-ops-cusum at the alarm.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Each step adds $x_t - 0.32$ and clips at 0.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#95de1ec4 .cell execution_count=20}
``` {.python .cell-code}
xs = np.array([0.30, 0.28, 0.33, 0.31, 0.36, 0.35, 0.37, 0.34, 0.38, 0.36])
path_, alarm_ = cusum(xs, 0.30, 0.02, 0.10)
print("S_t:", np.round(path_, 3), "alarm at index", alarm_)
z = xs - 0.32
best = max(z[s:alarm_ + 1].sum() for s in range(alarm_ + 1))
print(f"max over change points {best:.3f} = S at alarm {path_[alarm_]:.3f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
S_t: [0.   0.   0.01 0.   0.04 0.07 0.12 0.14 0.2  0.24] alarm at index 6
max over change points 0.120 = S at alarm 0.120
```
:::
:::


$S$ stays near zero for four batches, then grows by the excess above 0.32 at
every batch and crosses 0.1 at the seventh batch. The maximum over change
points equals $S_t$, attained by the stretch starting at the fifth batch —
CUSUM also says *when* the change probably began.
:::

::: {#exr-ops7-cusum-medium}
## Medium — tune h on a quiet stream
For the batch stream of this section (batches of 200 predictions, change at
150), estimate by simulation the mean number of batches between false alarms
(no change) and the mean detection delay, for $h \in \{0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2,
0.3\}$. Pick the smallest $h$ with at most one false alarm per 1 000 batches
on average, and report its delay.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Run in-control streams until the first alarm (cap at, say, 5 000 batches) to
estimate the average run length; start each delay simulation at the change.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#4a781fca .cell execution_count=21}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def run_length(p, h, k, cap=5000, rng=rng):
    s = 0.0
    for t in range(cap):
        s = max(0.0, s + rng.binomial(batch, p) / batch - p_neg_before - k)
        if s > h:
            return t + 1
    return cap

k_ = (p_neg_after - p_neg_before) / 2
for h in (0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.3):
    arl0 = np.mean([run_length(p_neg_before, h, k_) for _ in range(100)])
    delay = np.mean([run_length(p_neg_after, h, k_) for _ in range(200)])
    print(f"h = {h:.2f}: mean run without change {arl0:7.0f} batches (capped at 5000), mean delay {delay:5.1f} batches")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
h = 0.05: mean run without change      72 batches (capped at 5000), mean delay   2.3 batches
h = 0.10: mean run without change    1374 batches (capped at 5000), mean delay   4.0 batches
h = 0.15: mean run without change    4550 batches (capped at 5000), mean delay   5.6 batches
h = 0.20: mean run without change    5000 batches (capped at 5000), mean delay   7.1 batches
h = 0.30: mean run without change    4974 batches (capped at 5000), mean delay  10.2 batches
```
:::
:::


The run length without change grows very fast with $h$ while the delay grows
roughly linearly, as @prp-ops-cusum states. The smallest $h$ whose mean
quiet run exceeds 1 000 batches (here 0.1) is the operating point; its delay,
about four batches after the change, is the price of a monitor that can be
trusted. A threshold
chosen on a few days of history rather than by simulation is usually far too
low.
:::

::: {#exr-ops7-cusum-hard}
## Hard — a two-sided monitor for the class mix
Extend CUSUM to watch the share of **each** predicted class for increases
**and** decreases (six one-sided statistics), with a common threshold chosen
so that the combined monitor has a mean quiet run of at least 1 000 batches.
Test it on three changes: label shift towards negative, towards positive,
and the concept shift of @sec-ops-drift. Which statistic fires first in each
case?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
A decrease is an increase of $-x$: use $S^-_t = \max(0, S^-_{t-1} - x_t +
\mu_0 - k)$. The combined monitor alarms when any statistic does, so its quiet
run is shorter than each statistic's: tune $h$ on the combination.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#a2fd7196 .cell execution_count=22}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def class_monitor(stream, ref, k=0.015, h=0.2):
    s_up, s_down = np.zeros(3), np.zeros(3)
    for t, share in enumerate(stream):
        s_up = np.maximum(0, s_up + share - ref - k)
        s_down = np.maximum(0, s_down - share + ref - k)
        if (s_up > h).any() or (s_down > h).any():
            which = [f"{ob.LABELS[i]} up" for i in np.flatnonzero(s_up > h)] + \
                    [f"{ob.LABELS[i]} down" for i in np.flatnonzero(s_down > h)]
            return t, which
    return None, []

def shares_stream(n_batches, share):
    return [rng.multinomial(batch, share) / batch for _ in range(n_batches)]

h_star = None
for h in (0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.35, 0.4):                 # smallest h with a mean quiet run >= 1000 batches
    runs = [class_monitor(shares_stream(2000, ref_share), ref_share, h=h)[0] for _ in range(20)]
    mean_run = np.mean([2000 if t is None else t for t in runs])
    print(f"h = {h:.2f}: mean quiet run {mean_run:6.0f} batches (capped at 2000)")
    if h_star is None and mean_run >= 1000:
        h_star = h
targets = {"towards negative": {"prior": (0.4, 0.35, 0.25)}, "towards positive": {"prior": (0.25, 0.35, 0.4)},
           "concept shift": {"swap": {w: 0 for w in ("cheap", "fast", "smooth", "perfect", "awesome")}}}
for name, kw in targets.items():
    share = np.bincount(model.predict(ob.make_posts(5000, seed=790, **kw).text), minlength=3) / 5000
    t, which = class_monitor(shares_stream(500, share), ref_share, h=h_star)
    print(f"h = {h_star}: {name:17s} shares {np.round(share, 3)} -> alarm after {t} batches: {which}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
h = 0.20: mean quiet run    188 batches (capped at 2000)
h = 0.25: mean quiet run    822 batches (capped at 2000)
h = 0.30: mean quiet run   1832 batches (capped at 2000)
h = 0.35: mean quiet run   1932 batches (capped at 2000)
h = 0.40: mean quiet run   1998 batches (capped at 2000)
h = 0.3: towards negative  shares [0.403 0.35  0.247] -> alarm after 3 batches: ['negative up']
h = 0.3: towards positive  shares [0.257 0.361 0.382] -> alarm after 2 batches: ['positive up']
h = 0.3: concept shift     shares [0.241 0.407 0.353] -> alarm after 3 batches: ['positive up']
```
:::
:::


Six statistics at the threshold of a single one would raise false alarms
often (the first rows): the common threshold is chosen on the combination.
With it, both label shifts are detected within a few batches, and the
monitor names the class that moved. This concept shift is caught too, through
the shares it moves — here first as an increase of predicted positives: the
flipped words make posts that are now negative look positive. A concept shift that moves as many posts into a
class as out of it would leave the shares unchanged: for those, only labels
help.
:::

## Docker Compose, Prometheus, Grafana and alerts {#sec-ops-compose}

### A stack in one file

A monitoring setup is several programs — the service, Prometheus, an alert
router, a dashboard — that must start together, find each other by name, and
keep their data. **Docker Compose** describes such a multi-container
application in one YAML file: **services** (each an image and its
configuration), the **networks** that connect them (on the default network
each service is reachable under its own name), **volumes** for persistent
data, health checks and start-up order (`depends_on` with `condition:
service_healthy`) [@compose2026]. `docker compose up -d` creates and starts
everything; `down` removes it.


**`compose.yaml`**

``` {.yaml}
services:
  sentiment:
    build:
      context: ./service
      args:
        BASE: ${PYTHON_IMAGE:-python:3.12-slim}
    environment:
      MODEL_VERSION: "2026-11-18.1"
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:${SERVICE_PORT:-8000}:8000"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "python", "-c", "import urllib.request as u; u.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8000/ready', timeout=2)"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10

  prometheus:
    image: ${PROMETHEUS_IMAGE:-prom/prometheus:v3.16.0}
    command:
      - --config.file=/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml
      - --storage.tsdb.path=/prometheus
    volumes:
      - ./prometheus/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro
      - ./prometheus/rules.yml:/etc/prometheus/rules.yml:ro
      - prometheus-data:/prometheus
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:${PROMETHEUS_PORT:-9090}:9090"
    depends_on:
      sentiment:
        condition: service_healthy

  alertmanager:
    image: ${ALERTMANAGER_IMAGE:-prom/alertmanager:v0.35.0}
    command: ["--config.file=/etc/alertmanager/alertmanager.yml"]
    volumes:
      - ./alertmanager/alertmanager.yml:/etc/alertmanager/alertmanager.yml:ro
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:${ALERTMANAGER_PORT:-9093}:9093"

  grafana:
    image: grafana/grafana-oss:13.3.1
    profiles: ["dashboards"]            # started only with --profile dashboards
    volumes:
      - ./grafana/provisioning:/etc/grafana/provisioning:ro
      - ./grafana/dashboards:/var/lib/grafana/dashboards:ro
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:3000:3000"
    depends_on: [prometheus]

volumes:
  prometheus-data:
```



The images are the official ones by default; variables let the build machine
substitute local stand-ins (built from the binaries of the GitHub releases on
the local Ubuntu base of Part V) and choose free ports. The Grafana service
sits in a **profile**, so `docker compose up` starts it only when asked: the
build machine cannot download Grafana, and its part of the stack is configured
and validated below but not run.

### Rules: recording and alerting

Prometheus evaluates **rules** periodically. A **recording rule** stores the
result of an expression as a new series (cheap dashboards); an **alerting
rule** fires when its expression returns a value, after it has been true
continuously for the `for:` duration, and sends the alert to Alertmanager,
which groups, silences and routes notifications (e-mail, chat, paging)
[@prometheus2026]. Two alerts for the service, each with a threshold derived
from a number rather than chosen by feel:

- **error ratio**: more than 2 % of requests answered with 5xx over 5
  minutes — a burn rate of 4 for a 99.5 % SLO (@prp-ops-burn);
- **class mix**: the share of negative predictions over the last minute
  exceeds the reference share by more than four standard errors of a binomial
  proportion at the expected traffic. With reference share $\pi_0 \approx
  0\.30$ and about 1 200 predictions per minute,
  $\sqrt{\pi_0(1 - \pi_0)/1200} \approx 0.013$, so the threshold is
  $\pi_0 + 0.053$; `for: 30s` requires the condition to persist.


**`prometheus/rules.yml`**

``` {.yaml}
groups:
  - name: sentiment
    rules:
      - record: sentiment:negative_share:1m
        expr: >
          sum(rate(sentiment_predictions_total{label="negative"}[1m]))
          / sum(rate(sentiment_predictions_total[1m]))

      - alert: SentimentHighErrorRatio
        expr: >
          sum(rate(sentiment_http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
          / sum(rate(sentiment_http_requests_total[5m])) > 0.02
        for: 5m
        labels: {severity: page}
        annotations:
          summary: "More than 2% of requests fail (burn rate > 4 for a 99.5% SLO)"

      - alert: SentimentNegativeShareHigh
        expr: sentiment:negative_share:1m > 0.354
        for: 30s
        labels: {severity: ticket}
        annotations:
          summary: "Negative share {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} above reference + 4 standard errors"
```

``` {.python .cell-code}
    end, i = time.time() + duration, 0
    with httpx.Client(base_url=f"http://127.0.0.1:{SP}", timeout=5) as c:
```

### Testing alert rules

Alert rules are code, and can be unit-tested without waiting for incidents:
`promtool test rules` feeds synthetic series to the rules and checks which
alerts fire when [@prometheus2026]:


**`prometheus/tests.yml`**

``` {.yaml}
rule_files: [rules.yml]
evaluation_interval: 15s
tests:
  - interval: 15s
    input_series:
      # 100 requests per 15 s, of which 1 per 15 s fails from minute 0 (1 %), then 5 per 15 s from minute 10 (5 %)
      - series: 'sentiment_http_requests_total{path="/v1/predict", status="200"}'
        values: '0+99x40 3960+95x40'
      - series: 'sentiment_http_requests_total{path="/v1/predict", status="500"}'
        values: '0+1x40 40+5x40'
    alert_rule_test:
      - eval_time: 9m
        alertname: SentimentHighErrorRatio
        exp_alerts: []                       # 1 % < 2 %: quiet
      - eval_time: 14m
        alertname: SentimentHighErrorRatio
        exp_alerts: []                       # ratio above 2 % but not yet for 5 minutes
      - eval_time: 20m
        alertname: SentimentHighErrorRatio
        exp_alerts:
          - exp_labels: {severity: page}
            exp_annotations:
              summary: "More than 2% of requests fail (burn rate > 4 for a 99.5% SLO)"
```

### Grafana: dashboards and alerts as files

**Grafana** turns the series into dashboards: panels with PromQL queries,
thresholds and units, organised in a JSON document; it can also evaluate alert
rules itself and send notifications through contact points [@grafana2026].
Both can be **provisioned** from files, so that the dashboard is versioned with
the code instead of edited by hand: a data-source file tells Grafana where
Prometheus is, a dashboard provider loads JSON dashboards from a folder.


**`grafana/provisioning/datasources/prometheus.yml`**

``` {.yaml}
apiVersion: 1
datasources:
  - name: Prometheus
    uid: prometheus
    type: prometheus
    access: proxy
    url: http://prometheus:9090
    isDefault: true
```

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-ops7-compose-easy}
## Easy — a threshold from noise
The service handles 300 predictions per minute, of which 40 % are normally
neutral. An alert should fire when the neutral share over one minute drops
below normal by more than chance would explain. Compute a threshold at four
standard errors. If the share in successive minutes were independent, how
likely is a false alarm in a minute, and with `for: 3m` (three consecutive
one-minute evaluations)?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Standard error $\sqrt{0.4 \cdot 0.6/300}$; a normal variable is more than four
standard deviations below its mean with probability $\Phi(-4)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#a3c694ee .cell execution_count=31}
``` {.python .cell-code}
se = np.sqrt(0.4 * 0.6 / 300)
p_one = norm.cdf(-4)
print(f"threshold {0.4 - 4 * se:.3f}; P(false alarm in a minute) {p_one:.1e}; with for: 3m {p_one**3:.1e}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
threshold 0.287; P(false alarm in a minute) 3.2e-05; with for: 3m 3.2e-14
```
:::
:::


The threshold is about 0.287. With independent minutes, a single evaluation
crosses it about 3 times in 100 000, and three in a row essentially never.
Real evaluations are *not* independent — a rule evaluated every 5 s on a
1-minute window sees mostly the same data — so `for:` mainly suppresses short
spikes; the noise calculation is what sets the threshold.
:::

::: {#exr-ops7-compose-medium}
## Medium — unit-test the drift alert
Write `promtool` unit tests for `SentimentNegativeShareHigh`: synthetic
`sentiment_predictions_total` series in which the negative share is at the
reference level for ten minutes and then rises above the threshold. Check that
the alert does not fire before the rise, does not fire 15 seconds after it
(the `for:` duration has not elapsed), and fires a minute after.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Counters grow by a constant per interval: `'0+30x40 1200+60x20'` means +30
per interval for 40 intervals, then +60 per interval. The recording rule needs
a full minute of data after the change to reflect it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution


**`prometheus/tests_drift.yml`**

``` {.yaml}
rule_files: [rules.yml]
evaluation_interval: 15s
tests:
  - interval: 15s
    input_series:
      # per 15 s: 30 negative, 40 neutral, 30 positive; from minute 10: 60 negative
      - series: 'sentiment_predictions_total{label="negative"}'
        values: '0+30x40 1200+60x20'
      - series: 'sentiment_predictions_total{label="neutral"}'
        values: '0+40x60'
      - series: 'sentiment_predictions_total{label="positive"}'
        values: '0+30x60'
    alert_rule_test:
      - eval_time: 9m
        alertname: SentimentNegativeShareHigh
        exp_alerts: []
      - eval_time: 10m15s
        alertname: SentimentNegativeShareHigh
        exp_alerts: []
      - eval_time: 12m
        alertname: SentimentNegativeShareHigh
        exp_alerts:
          - exp_labels: {severity: ticket}
```


``` {.bash}
$ promtool test rules tests_drift.yml
```

```
Processing test file: tests_drift.yml


  FAILED:
    alertname: SentimentNegativeShareHigh, time: 12m, 
        exp:[
            0:
              Labels:{alertname="SentimentNegativeShareHigh", severity="ticket"}
              Annotations:{}
            ], 
        got:[
            0:
              Labels:{alertname="SentimentNegativeShareHigh", severity="ticket"}
              Annotations:{summary="Negative share 46.15% above reference + 4 standard errors"}
            ]
[exit status 1]
```



Before the change the share is 0.30 and nothing fires; 15 seconds after it,
the one-minute rate has barely moved and the `for:` clock has not run out;
two minutes after it the share is $60/130 \approx 0.46$, above the threshold,
and the alert fires. The test fails if someone "simplifies" the recording rule
or raises the threshold without noticing — which is the point.
:::

::: {#exr-ops7-compose-hard}
## Hard — an alert on concept drift?
Concept shift is invisible to label-free signals (@exr-ops7-drift-hard).
Design an alert that can catch it in production: what extra data must flow
into the monitoring (and from where), which metric does Prometheus compute,
what threshold and window would you use given that only 20 labelled posts
arrive per hour, and how long would it take to detect a drop of accuracy from
0.93 to 0.85? Implement the metric as two counters in the service (a
`POST /v1/feedback` endpoint receiving the true label of a previously
classified post) and test the alert with promtool.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Count feedback events and correct predictions; accuracy over a window is
`increase(correct[6h]) / increase(feedback[6h])`. With 20 labels per hour, a
6-hour window has 120 labels: use the test-size reasoning of
@sec-ops-model-tests to set the threshold.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#b2a28cf2 .cell execution_count=33}
``` {.python .cell-code}
n_lab = 120                                         # labels in a 6-hour window
p0, p1 = 0.93, 0.85
thr_acc = p0 - norm.ppf(0.99) * np.sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / n_lab)
power = norm.cdf((thr_acc - p1) / np.sqrt(p1 * (1 - p1) / n_lab))
print(f"threshold {thr_acc:.3f} (1% false alarms per window), power against 0.85 = {power:.2f}")
ob.write("prometheus/rules_feedback.yml", f"""
    groups:
      - name: quality
        rules:
          - alert: SentimentAccuracyDrop
            expr: >
              increase(sentiment_feedback_correct_total[6h]) / increase(sentiment_feedback_total[6h]) < {thr_acc:.3f}
              and increase(sentiment_feedback_total[6h]) >= 60
            for: 1h
            labels: {{severity: ticket}}
""", base=stack)
ob.write("prometheus/tests_feedback.yml", """
    rule_files: [rules_feedback.yml]
    evaluation_interval: 5m
    tests:
      - interval: 5m
        input_series:                          # 20 labels/hour = 5 per 15 min; accuracy 0.93 then 0.8
          - series: sentiment_feedback_total
            values: '0+1.6667x200'
          - series: sentiment_feedback_correct_total
            values: '0+1.55x100 155+1.3333x100'
        alert_rule_test:
          - eval_time: 8h
            alertname: SentimentAccuracyDrop
            exp_alerts: []
          - eval_time: 16h
            alertname: SentimentAccuracyDrop
            exp_alerts:
              - exp_labels: {severity: ticket}
""", base=stack)
p = ob.run(f"cd prometheus && {ob.tool('promtool')} test rules tests_feedback.yml", cwd=stack)
print(ob.mask(p.stdout.strip() or p.stderr.strip()))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
threshold 0.876 (1% false alarms per window), power against 0.85 = 0.79
Processing test file: tests_feedback.yml
  SUCCESS
```
:::
:::


The extra data are **delayed labels**: a sample of classified posts sent to
annotators (or user feedback such as "this label is wrong"), joined back to
the prediction by an identifier and posted to the service, which counts
feedback and correct predictions — the service already knows what it
predicted. With 120 labels per window, a threshold at 1 % false alarms is
about 0.875, and a drop to 0.85 is caught in a single window about four times
in five; detecting it with near certainty takes a longer window or more
labels per hour. The rule also requires a minimum
number of labels, so that a quiet night does not fire it. The promtool test
checks that the alert stays quiet while accuracy is 0.93 and fires once a
drop to 0.8 has filled the window and persisted for the `for:` duration.
:::

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch out
- **Monitoring only the service**: a model can be up, fast and wrong.
- **Summaries instead of histograms** when replicas must be aggregated;
  histogram buckets far from the thresholds that matter.
- **PSI thresholds as laws**: they depend on binning and ignore sample size.
- **A test per window at 5 %**: daily false alarms; correct for multiplicity
  or accumulate evidence (CUSUM).
- **The share of predictions as the share of classes**: correct for the
  classifier's errors (BBSE, EM) — and check the label-shift assumption.
- **No labels at all**: concept shift stays invisible.
- **Alerts without tests, dashboards edited by hand**: version and test them.
:::

## Summary

- Monitor four layers: service (golden signals), inputs, outputs, quality.
  SLOs and error budgets turn reliability into numbers; burn rate $r =
  e/(1-s)$ says how fast the budget goes.
- Prometheus scrapes counters, gauges and histograms; `histogram_quantile`
  interpolates inside a bucket, with error at most the bucket's width.
- Shift is covariate, label or concept. PSI $= \mathrm{KL}(p\|q) +
  \mathrm{KL}(q\|p)$ measures size and shrinks with coarser bins; KS with the
  DKW–Massart bound gives windows of $n > 8\ln(4/\alpha)/\delta^2$; Pearson's
  $\chi^2$ tests the class mix. Many windows need multiplicity control.
- Under label shift, $q = C^{-1}\mu$ (BBSE) and EM on calibrated probabilities
  estimate the class mix without labels; both fail under concept shift, which
  only labels reveal.
- CUSUM $S_t = \max(0, S_{t-1} + x_t - \mu_0 - k)$ maximises over change
  points; delay grows linearly and the quiet run exponentially with $h$.
- Docker Compose runs the service, Prometheus and Alertmanager together;
  rules and dashboards are files — validated with promtool and against the
  live Prometheus.

## Exercises

::: {#exr-ops7-length-oov}
**An unknown-word monitor.** Slang was the shift that label-free monitors
barely saw. Add a metric for the share of words in each text that are not in
the model's vocabulary, and show on windows of 500 posts that a KS test on it
detects the slang shift that the length and confidence monitors missed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#9975cfd5 .cell execution_count=34}
``` {.python .cell-code}
vocab = set(model[0].vocabulary_)
def oov_share(texts):
    out = []
    for t in texts:
        words = re.findall(r"\b\w+\b", t.lower())
        out.append(np.mean([w not in vocab for w in words]) if words else 0.0)
    return np.array(out)
ref_oov = oov_share(reference.text)
for name, kw in (("none", {}), ("covariate: unseen slang", {"slang_rate": 0.8})):
    pvals = [ks_2samp(ref_oov, oov_share(ob.make_posts(500, seed=950 + i, **kw).text)).pvalue for i in range(30)]
    print(f"{name:24s} detection rate at 1 %: {np.mean(np.array(pvals) < 0.01):.2f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
none                     detection rate at 1 %: 0.00
covariate: unseen slang  detection rate at 1 %: 1.00
```
:::
:::


The unknown-word share jumps when slang appears and the KS test catches it in
essentially every window, while staying quiet without shift. Monitors should
target the *mechanism* by which a shift hurts the model: unseen words are
exactly what a bag-of-words model cannot use.
:::

::: {#exr-ops7-psi-n}
**PSI and sample size.** Compute the distribution of the PSI of the
confidence (10 quantile bins) between a reference of 5 000 posts and windows
of 200, 1 000 and 10 000 posts **from the same distribution**. What fraction
of windows exceed the folklore threshold 0.1 in each case?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#65b95811 .cell execution_count=35}
``` {.python .cell-code}
for n in (200, 1000, 10_000):
    vals = []
    for i in range(30):
        conf = model.predict_proba(ob.make_posts(n, seed=1000 + 31 * i + n).text).max(1)
        p_b = np.maximum(np.bincount(np.searchsorted(edges, conf), minlength=10) / n, 1e-6)
        vals.append(np.sum((p_b - q_bins) * np.log(p_b / q_bins)))
    print(f"n = {n:6d}: median PSI {np.median(vals):.4f}, share above 0.1: {np.mean(np.array(vals) > 0.1):.2f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
n =    200: median PSI 0.0417, share above 0.1: 0.00
n =   1000: median PSI 0.0090, share above 0.1: 0.00
n =  10000: median PSI 0.0015, share above 0.1: 0.00
```
:::
:::


Without any shift, the PSI of small windows is inflated by sampling noise
(its expectation is roughly $(B - 1)(1/n + 1/N)$ for $B$ bins); with 200
posts the median is several times that of 10 000 posts. A fixed threshold
therefore means different things at different traffic levels — the reason to
pair a size measure with a test.
:::

::: {#exr-ops7-burn-windows}
**Two-window burn-rate alert.** Write a PromQL alert that fires when the error
budget of a 99.5 % SLO burns at more than 14.4 times the sustainable rate over
both the last hour and the last 5 minutes, and test with promtool that it
fires during a spike of 50 % errors lasting 15 minutes but not for a 2-minute
spike of the same intensity.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#98791b0b .cell execution_count=36}
``` {.python .cell-code}
ob.write("prometheus/rules_burn.yml", """
    groups:
      - name: slo
        rules:
          - alert: SentimentBudgetBurn
            expr: >
              (sum(rate(sentiment_http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[1h])) / sum(rate(sentiment_http_requests_total[1h]))) > 14.4 * 0.005
              and
              (sum(rate(sentiment_http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(sentiment_http_requests_total[5m]))) > 14.4 * 0.005
            labels: {severity: page}
""", base=stack)
ok_per_min, err_per_min = np.full(260, 100), np.zeros(260, int)     # 100 requests per minute
for start, length in ((60, 2), (180, 15)):                           # 50 % errors: 2 min at 60, 15 min at 180
    ok_per_min[start:start + length], err_per_min[start:start + length] = 50, 50
series = lambda inc: " ".join(map(str, np.r_[0, np.cumsum(inc)]))
ob.write("prometheus/tests_burn.yml", f"""
    rule_files: [rules_burn.yml]
    evaluation_interval: 1m
    tests:
      - interval: 1m
        input_series:
          - series: 'sentiment_http_requests_total{{status="200"}}'
            values: '{series(ok_per_min)}'
          - series: 'sentiment_http_requests_total{{status="500"}}'
            values: '{series(err_per_min)}'
        alert_rule_test:
          - eval_time: 63m
            alertname: SentimentBudgetBurn
            exp_alerts: []
          - eval_time: 194m
            alertname: SentimentBudgetBurn
            exp_alerts:
              - exp_labels: {{severity: page}}
""", base=stack)
p = ob.run(f"cd prometheus && {ob.tool('promtool')} test rules tests_burn.yml", cwd=stack)
print(ob.mask(p.stdout.strip() or p.stderr.strip()))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
Processing test file: tests_burn.yml
  SUCCESS
```
:::
:::


The 1-hour window ignores the short spike (2 minutes at 50 % average to
under 2 % over an hour, below the 7.2 % that a burn rate of 14.4 means) while
the 5-minute window alone would have paged for it; during the long spike both
windows exceed 7.2 %, and the 5-minute window lets the alert stop soon after
the incident ends. Requiring both makes the alert significant and quick to
reset. A 15-minute spike of 10 % errors, by contrast, consumes less than 1 % of
a month's budget and should not page anyone.
:::
